nodes.label: Barbell flat bench press
Bilateral standing cable fly at shoulder height
Studies disagree about whether changing your grip width changes how hard the chest muscle works.

Raising the bench usually takes work away from the lower chest, though not in every study that measured it. Whether it adds work to the upper chest is not settled: the best single study suggests a peak around 30 degrees rather than a steady increase, and pooled evidence finds no clear upper-chest difference at all.
The chest muscle works during a barbell bench press, both its upper and lower parts.
Tearing the chest muscle's tendon is a recognised injury that has been reported to happen while bench pressing.
As the bar goes up, the leverage the weight has over the shoulder falls the whole way, while the leverage over the elbow is smallest at the hardest point of the lift.
The elbow bends and straightens much less in a cable cross-over than in a bench press.
For the same relative load, a standing cable cross-over put a larger turning force on the shoulder joint than a flat barbell bench press.
The upper part of the chest muscle works during a dumbbell fly.
There is one published report of someone tearing the chest muscle off the arm bone while using a chest fly machine.
Two months of pec deck training made the chest muscle thicker than doing nothing.
In one study, people who trained with compound lifts gained more bench press strength than people who trained with isolation lifts, but their body composition changed the same amount.
Of all the shoulder muscles, the chest muscle has some of the best leverage for pulling the upper arm down and across the body.
The chest muscle runs from the collarbone, breastbone and upper rib cartilages to a narrow attachment on the upper arm bone.
A study that imaged and then sectioned the same fourteen shoulders found a single-layer attachment, not the two-layer attachment usually described.
Where the chest muscle attaches to the arm bone, the attachment is long from top to bottom but very narrow from side to side.
In two small studies, about two months of chest training made the chest muscle measurably thicker.
Two main nerves supply the chest muscle, an upper one and a lower one, but dissection studies find the pattern varies from person to person and that other nerves contribute too.
The chest muscle is usually described as having an upper part from the collarbone and a larger lower part from the breastbone and ribs, plus a small lowest part.
Change the angle your arm works at and you change which part of the chest muscle does most of the work.
Different parts of the chest muscle do measurably different amounts of work, and which part works hardest depends on the movement.
Roughly one chest muscle in three differs in some way from the textbook description.
The usual way of measuring chest-muscle activity with skin electrodes does not represent the whole muscle, and the measurement point effectively moves during a bench press.
Studies that compared chest-muscle activity between a bench press and a fly disagree. Some find the press higher, several find no difference, and the pooled evidence is too inconsistent to settle it.
